title: John Oliver Brutally Mocks Trump for Sacrificing Staff in Airplane-Swap Incident
description: On Sunday night, the summer’s hottest soap opera star, John Oliver, opened the latest edition of his Emmy-winning HBO series “Last Week Tonight” by
body:
On Sunday night, the summer’s hottest soap opera star, John Oliver, opened the latest edition of his Emmy-winning HBO series “Last Week Tonight” by addressing Trump’s controversial airplane switcheroo incident whilst leaving a NATO summit in Turkey.

	“The Iran War dragged on with a series of humiliating news headlines including this revelation about Trump’s trip home from last month’s NATO summit,” offered Oliver.


	Yes, Trump’s plane was secretly swapped out on his return trip from Turkey owing to intelligence regarding a possible Iranian attempt on his Qatari-gifted Air Force One plane. Trump reportedly snuck out of the plane and onto a catering truck that whisked him off to a smaller military jet for the return flight.  
	

	“Fantastic. The only problem I can see there is: Next time he needs to escape, he’s not going to be able to use the catering truck trick again because everyone knows about it now,” cracked Oliver. “People are going to be suspicious from now on if they see a plane go one way, a catering truck go another and an enormous man-sized cake get wheeled away by two suspiciously-jacked chefs.”

	“While it clearly doesn’t look great for a president to be emergency-hiding in a catering truck, it looks even worse when you remember that a lot of other people were still on that plane that he was smuggled off of,” continued Oliver.

	Yes, a number of journalists and White House staffers, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, were left onboard Air Force One after Trump escaped.
	

	“Not great!” exclaimed Oliver. “There were a lot of innocent people on that plane — and Marco Rubio.”

	Coincidentally — or not — Trump’s White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt announced her resignation shortly after the airplane-swap incident.

schema.headline: John Oliver Brutally Mocks Trump for Sacrificing Staff in Airplane-Swap Incident

title: Hayden Panettiere, ‘Heroes’ and ‘Scream’ Star, Dies at 36
description: Hayden Panettiere, known for her roles on “Heroes,” “Nashville” and in “Scream 4” and “Scream VI,” died on Sunday. Her rep confirmed her death to AB
body:
Hayden Panettiere, known for her roles on “Heroes,” “Nashville” and in “Scream 4” and “Scream VI,” died on Sunday. Her rep confirmed her death to ABC News. A cause of death was not immediately known.

	“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen,” her rep told ABC.
	

	Panettiere had been on screen since 1994, at age 5, starting on soap operas “One Life to Live” — appearing on 27 episodes — and later, “Guiding Light,” starring on 45. In 2000, she landed a breakout role in “Remember the Titans,” and in 2006, she joined the cast of “Heroes” as Claire Bennett, portraying the cheerleader in 73 episodes of the NBC drama.


	Panettiere later earned two Golden Globe nominations for playing Juliette Barnes on “Nashville.” She starred in 128 episodes from 2012 to 2018.

	On the film side, she is most known for her role as Kirby in 2011’s “Scream 4.” She became such a fan favorite that she was then asked to return for 2023’s “Scream VI.” She also co-starred with Michelle Trachtenberg in “Ice Princess” and appeared in “Bring It On: All or Nothing.”

	Raised in Palisades, N.Y., her mother was a soap opera actress and her father was a fire captain. As a child, she appeared on shows including “Ally McBeal” and “Malcolm in the Middle.”

	Panettiere published her first book, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” in May of this year. In it, she shared many stories from her life in the limelight, including details of her troubled relationship with her mother and abuse she endured through her life in Hollywood.
	

	She had also been open through the years about her struggle with alcohol and drugs. In 2020, she spent time at a rehab facility and got sober. In 2023, her younger brother Jansen died unexpectedly of a heart condition at 28. “When something that massive has happened to you, you really learn to pick your fights and just not let the little things upset you,” she told People magazine in 2024 about the death. “Because once something so horrific, so deep, so catastrophic happens in your life, there’s not much that can really rock you.”

	She made headlines following the People interview, when fans voiced concerns over her slurred speech, something she later spoke about via an Instagram post. “I hadn’t slept for two days prior to the shoot due to one of my dogs who was recovering from an emergency surgical procedure,” she shared at the time, also responding to claims about medication she may be on. “I was exhausted. My rep stopped the interview early as it became obvious that I was fading — especially as the subject matter became heavier… Grief looks different on everyone. Whether or not I am on medication is none of anyone’s business and is between me and my doctor.”

	She continued, “Mental health is so important, and I hope those reading this now understand that what you say hiding behind a computer screen can have a detrimental impact on someone.”

	She had a daughter, Kaya, with boxer Wladimir Klitschko, who retained custody due to Panettiere’s struggles with addiction and postpartum depression.

schema.headline: Hayden Panettiere, ‘Heroes’ and ‘Scream’ Star, Dies at 36

title: Noah Wyle Hopes David Ellison’s Threat to Move Paramount Out of California is ‘Saber Rattling’: ‘You’re Going to Take Hollywood Out of Hollywood’
description:
Noah Wyle is hoping David Ellison isn’t serious about moving Paramount out of California.

	“I hope this is saber rattling because I can’t think of
body:
Noah Wyle is hoping David Ellison isn’t serious about moving Paramount out of California.

	“I hope this is saber rattling because I can’t think of anything that would less engender you to the population of this industry than to say you’re going to take Hollywood out of Hollywood,” the “Pitt” star told me Sunday at the HBO Max Emmy Nominee Celebration in Los Angeles. “But I’m an Angeleno, so I have a vested interest in that one.”
	

	Variety confirmed on Aug. 11 that Ellison is prepared to start moving Paramount out of California as soon as October unless the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger is resolved through a settlement with the state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta. Twelve states have filed an antitrust case to block the merger.


	Paramount hasn’t yet decided where its new home might be; the company is considering destinations including Georgia, Texas and Tennessee.

	In March, Wyle spoke at a hearing organized by California Sen. Adam Schiff, held at City Hall in Burbank, in support of tax incentives to bring film and TV production back to the state. “I was asked to participate in today’s hearing to tell a success story,” Wyle said, according to the Associated Press. “I’m happy to report we’ll commence shooting season three this summer, and that a rising tide has indeed lifted all boats.”

	“The Pitt” shoots on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank. Wyle said the first season of the HBO series created 600 production jobs and brought $125 million to the state economy.

	At the Emmy Nominee Celebration, Wyle said he couldn’t predict what would happen with the merger.
	

	“One article that says this, one article says that, one rumor leads you to believe one thing,” he said. “They haven’t painted the place yet, so who knows.”

schema.headline: Noah Wyle Hopes David Ellison’s Threat to Move Paramount Out of California is ‘Saber Rattling’: ‘You’re Going to Take Hollywood Out of Hollywood’

title: Dwayne Johnson Leads Crowd in ‘Happy Birthday’ Song for Daughter Simone After Receiving Disney Legends Award at D23
description:
Dwayne Johnson has been officially crowned a legend — a Disney Legend that is. 

	On Sunday at D23, Johnson was honored with the hall-of-fame-style
body:
Dwayne Johnson has been officially crowned a legend — a Disney Legend that is. 

	On Sunday at D23, Johnson was honored with the hall-of-fame-style award from the Walt Disney Company. From “Jungle Cruise” to the “Moana” franchise and “Race to Witch Mountain,” Johnson is no stranger to the world of Disney. But as he took the stage to receive the honor, Johnson emphasized that his most important role is that of father. 


	During his off-the-cuff speech, Johnson recalled the first time he took his eldest daughter Simone to Disneyland. She was five years old, and they had breakfast with the princesses.
	

	“I was in my 20s … I was trying to figure that stuff out at that time: how I was going to be a father, how I was going to be a husband, man, etc,” he recalled. “But I remember one of the princesses said, ‘Close your eyes and make a wish.’ And I’ll never forget, [Simone] closed her eyes and she made a wish.”

	Johnson continued, getting a little emotional at the memory: “I just remember that moment on my daughter’s face. I had never seen that before. She was just so into making a wish. … I said, ‘God, I wonder what was going through the little mind.’ And it’s just experiences like that that we create that I know she’ll never forget. I’ll never forget. That’s the beauty of Disney. That’s the beauty also of being a Disney Legend.”

	As it turns out, the Disney Legends ceremony took place just after Simone’s 25th birthday, so he led the full arena in a “Happy Birthday” tribute to her. 


	During his emotional remarks, Johnson also shouted out his younger daughters, Jasmine and Tiana, who were watching at home. “They asked me, ‘What does it mean to be a Disney Legend?'” he recalled. “I said, ‘Well, it means we get free tickets.'”
	

	Johnson was presented with his Disney Legends award by his “Jungle Cruise” and “The Smashing Machine” co-star Emily Blunt, who made a surprise appearance at the award to wax poetic about her friend.

	“When I first met Dwayne Johnson, I had assumed wrongly that he would have the energy of a man who was a sort of walking suplex,” Blunt said. “But the bravado of ‘The Rock’ was actually nowhere to be seen.” Johnson’s persona as “The Rock” is just a performance, she explained. “It’s the performance of a lifetime

	“What I was met with was someone who was so disarmingly wise, gentle, curious, totally unpretentious,” Blunt continued. “And not to say this one’s an angel, all right, because he’s not. He’s a non-conforming, rule-breaking, mold-breaking rebel.”

Emily Blunt calls Dwayne Johnson “disarmingly wise, gentle, curious and totally unpretentious” while honoring him as a Disney Legend at #D23: “And that’s not to say this one’s an angel, all right, because he’s not. He’s a non-conforming, rule-breaking, mold-breaking rebel.” pic.twitter.com/fBwRhIyFq6— Variety (@Variety) August 16, 2026


	This summer, Johnson brought “Moana” back to the big screen for a live-action voyage and reprised his role as the demi-god Maui. In the lead-up to the movie’s debut, Johnson spoke about bringing Pacific Islander culture to the masses, and why the “Moana” cinematic universe matters for representation and visibility. Johnson, who also produced the movie, said he didn’t see himself represented in media when he was growing up: “‘Indiana Jones’ inspired me. When I was 8 years old watching Harrison Ford, I was like, ‘I want to be that guy,’ but that guy didn’t look like me.”

	As mentioned, the “Moana” movies are just part of Johnson’s legacy with the company. In 2024, Seven Bucks Productions, the film and TV content label founded by Johnson and Dany Garcia, signed a first-look deal with The Walt Disney Company to develop films for theatrical and streaming. Last year, 20th Television closed a first-look TV deal with the company.

	The Disney Legends Awards program is a 39-year tradition of The Walt Disney Company, which began when Fred MacMurray (“The Shaggy Dog,” “The Absent-Minded Professor,” “The Happiest Millionaire”) was honored in 1987. Including this year’s honorees, a total of 329 Disney Legends have been named.

	The 2026 Disney Legends honorees include former Disney chairman and CEO Bob Iger, Anne Hathaway, Susan Egan and Alan Tudyk, for bringing “unforgettable characters to life on-screen and on-stage.” The Jonas brothers are being honored for “shaping a generation of Disney music,” Lin‑Manuel Miranda for “groundbreaking songwriting for modern Disney favorites” and Eric Goldberg for his “artistry and animation.”
	

	Past Disney Legends include Tim Allen, Dame Julie Andrews, Angela Bassett, Tony Baxter, Kristen Bell, James Cameron, Jamie Lee Curtis, Miley Cyrus, Marc Davis, Robert Downey Jr., Harrison Ford, Annette Funicello, Josh Gad, Whoopi Goldberg, Jonathan Groff, Steve Jobs, Sir Elton John, Dame Angela Lansbury, Stan Lee, George Lucas, Steve Martin, Burny Mattinson, Alan Menken, Idina Menzel, Hayley Mills, Fess Parker, Ellen Pompeo, Robin Roberts, the Sherman Brothers, Marty Sklar, Dick Van Dyke, Barbara Walters, Betty White, John Williams, Robin Williams and Oprah Winfrey.

schema.headline: Dwayne Johnson Leads Crowd in ‘Happy Birthday’ Song for Daughter Simone After Receiving Disney Legends Award at D23

title: ‘The End of Tom Six’ Review: The Director of the ‘Human Centipede’ Films Has Multiple Sclerosis and Is Sharing the Horror. This Confessional Doc Is His Witty Self-Defense
description: Yesterday’s punk, grunge, and rebel-outsider upstarts have an uncanny way of evolving into today’s elder statesmen of respectable infamy. (Hello, Jo
body:
Yesterday’s punk, grunge, and rebel-outsider upstarts have an uncanny way of evolving into today’s elder statesmen of respectable infamy. (Hello, John Waters, Patti Smith, John Lydon, Henry Rollins, and Robin Byrd.) But it’s doubtful that Tom Six will ever be in the mix of latter-day prestige. His desire to stand apart from it is too great.

	In case he’s not on your radar, Tom Six is the Dutch director of the “Human Centipede” trilogy, a series of horror films so grotesque that the idea of sitting through them would be a deal-breaker for 97 percent of moviegoers. Six was after the other three percent: the kind who feed off shock and transgression, and who recognize that a horror movie that makes hardened veterans of the genre feel like they have to watch parts of it peeking between their fingers is either a movie that has gone too far…or one that’s the definition of what true horror is. The “Human Centipede” trilogy — especially “The Human Centipede 2 (Full Sequence),” a hellacious “Götterdämmerung” of torture porn — was both.
	

	Released in 2009, 2011, and 2015 (and watched mostly on VOD), the “Human Centipede” films carved out an extreme niche on the edge of global movie culture. Yet they also found a perverse mainstream foothold, becoming a cheeky meme (sorry! pun intended) referenced on “South Park,” “The Simpsons,” “Saturday Night Live,” “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt,” “Deadpool 2,” “Beavis and Butt-Head,” and the Childish Gambino video for “Bonfire.” Tom Mix wasn’t aiming for respectability; he was going as far as possible in the opposite direction. But he was courting notoriety and fame, and he did it by working in the carny-barker freak-show tradition of exploitation-world self-marketers like Herschell Gordon Lewis, Russ Meyer, Ted V. Mikels, and (of course) John Waters. These were filmmakers who specialized in selling a vibe of on-the-fringe danger, creating an underground mystique that was part of what made them successful. (By the time Waters was done peddling “Pink Flamingos” on the midnight-movie circuit, he had made a fortune, which became the basis of his trash-art empire.)
	

	“The End of Tom Six” is about how Tom Six made and sold his films in the same spirit. But it’s also about how his dark dream came crashing down. The movie, which premieres this weekend on YouTube, is a DIY schlock- umentary that’s also a real documentary, one that captures how Six’s life became his own private horror film, after he was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.

	He first learned that he had the condition 14 years ago, and for a long time he was able to manage its symptoms comfortably (and in secret). But MS is incurable and progressive. For the last six years, Six has lived as a recluse in Amsterdam, lying in bed and going out twice a day for decaf coffee (the regular brew is too hard on his shattered nerves). “The End of Tom Six” is a self-styled confessional memoir in which Six fuses his life and career and illness into a kind of parable. He’s asking: Is there room anymore for movies like his, that stray over the line? And if not, what does that mean?

	Shot in black-and-white, “The End of Tom Six” opens with noirish images of an Amsterdam canal, lined with street lamps that look straight out of the London of “Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.” The images are accompanied by a doomy romantic Hollywood/classical score, and then, in old-fashioned letters, the words “The End” appear (with the added words “…of Tom Six”). So this will be the story of the end of Tom Six’s life. But it’s really the story of how he made his movies, and sold his image, and is still doing it, to the point that you may wonder at moments if his battle with MS is actually an Andy Kaufman stunt. (I don’t think it is; but one wouldn’t put it past him.)

	The film moves inside Six’s home, where he’s lying in a paisley silk bathrobe on an antique Chinese opium bed, wearing a dandified mustache and Panama hat and dark aviator shades, smoking a Havana cigar, looking like Hunter Thompson’s hip Euro brother crossed with Michael O’Donoghue crossed with a svelte version of Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Mix is surrounded by a small crew and entourage: his paramour, Marci (Maartje Willems), who beams and insinuates like Morticia Addams; the film’s megaphone-wielding director, also played by Six; the camera man, boom operator, and butler, all played by the dwarf actor Edwin Alofs; a uniformed Nazi (Servaes Nelissen) who’s on hand to gloweringly comb the proceedings for trigger warnings and ideas worthy of censorship; and a first assistant director (Demian Kurosa) who looks like a circus tattooed man and talks with a post-operative vocoder.
	

	Six keeps cutting between himself and this kitsch gallery of jokers, tossing in B-movie “All About Eve” exchanges (“Alcohol is killing you slowly, baby.” “That’s okay, I’m not in a hurry”), which keeps the tone light. It also purges the movie of self-pity and helps to break up what is basically an amusing and irascibly witty Tom Six monologue of self-justification. Is “The End of Tom Six” for fans only? No question. But I count myself among the three percent who watched “The Human Centipede 2” and found it to contain a hint of the awesome within its awfulness, the same way I felt when I read the Marquis de Sade’s “The 120 Days of Sodom.” These are not works you recommend to people. But they’re works that, in their sick way, might be said to expand one’s vision of human evil.

	I was interested, after 15 years, to discover what sort of dude Tom Six is, and to hear him explain to his audience why he made these movies, and about how it shaped his experience (“To this day, I get marriage proposals and death threats”), and to listen to his diary of debilitating illness. “The End of Tom Six” is not a work of true-life body horror. Six describes his symptoms, and drug regimen (Oxycodone for the chronic pain), with tough understatement. At one point, though, he does admit, “I’m a fucking living X-ray. I’ve got massive brain fog from all the medications. My thoughts are like scrambled eggs.”

	What he wants to talk about is the movie he made after the “Human Centipede” trilogy. It’s called “The Onania Club,” and it’s the story of a group of chic women in Los Angeles (Chloë Sevigny is one of the stars) who get aroused by the misery and suffering of others. It is, as Six describes it, a story about the opposite of empathy. But in that sense, it’s about the loss of empathy, and maybe the end of it.

	Tom Six made “The Onania Club” in 2019, and though he had struggled to find a distributor for “The Human Centipede” and its sequels, he eventually did. With those films having crossed over into the pop consciousness, he figured he’d have no problem nailing down a distributor for a movie less grotesque and more serious. But no distributor would touch it. What he kept hearing was “The marketplace has changed.” In other words, no one wanted to deal with the controversy that might rear its head in an increasingly censorious environment. Six claims that the stress of all this exacerbated his illness. The way he portrays it, his health disaster was the crucifixion a clampdown society helped to reinforce. We’ll have to take his word on that. But while I haven’t seen “The Onania Club” (it remains unreleased), and therefore can’t comment on it, I will say this much. “The End of Tom Six,” an underground-cinephile-on-acid curio, is worth seeing for the question it raises: Do we want the arena of cinema to be a place where anything can happen, or do we want it to be a safe space?

schema.headline: ‘The End of Tom Six’ Review: The Director of the ‘Human Centipede’ Films Has Multiple Sclerosis and Is Sharing the Horror. This Confessional Doc Is His Witty Self-Defense

title: Bob Iger Gets All-Star Send-Off From Robert Downey Jr., Harrison Ford and New CEO Josh D’Amaro at D23 Disney Legends Ceremony
description:
Bob Iger is officially a legend within the Disney kingdom.

	We can’t call it surprising that the media giant named its former CEO (twice over) to i
body:
Bob Iger is officially a legend within the Disney kingdom.

	We can’t call it surprising that the media giant named its former CEO (twice over) to its hall of fame, but it’s certainly fitting. Iger, 75, has guided the company to delirious heights of success – and through some of its darkest ever hours.

	Disney insiders said Iger is the first executive to ever be named an official “Disney Legend,” joining a 2026 class that includes Anne Hathaway (“The Princess Diaries,” “The Devil Wears Prada” franchise) and Lin-Manuel Miranda (“Mary Poppins Returns,” “Moana”).
	

	Iger was introduced by his CEO successor, Josh D’Amaro, who officially took over as the head of Disney in March. Robert Downey Jr., Harrison Ford, Ellen Pompeo, Diane Sawyer and others also took the stage to honor Iger and reminisce about his impact on the Mouse House. 


	“What I’ve always admired the most about Bob is not necessarily what he’s accomplished; it is who he is,” D’Amaro said. “He leans with integrity. He leans with optimism. He treats everyone with respect, and he cares deeply about people, about Disney, and about the stories that we share in the whole world. I’ve been fortunate to get to work alongside him, and his friendship has meant more than I can say.”

	“Fortune favors the brave,” said Downey Jr. “To me, those four words explain Mr. Iger’s primary quality: it’s courage. It’s the bold choices in the face of incredible risk, trusting your instincts, empowering people to aspire beyond their limitations. And as he closes this chapter and begins the next, somehow, somehow, seems like he’s still just only getting started. That is, Bob, why you truly are the legend in every sense of the word.”
	

	“Now, over the years, I’ve had the privilege of giving this award out to dozens and dozens of truly worthy people, unbelievably talented people who contributed so much to this company, and so it is an incredible honor for me to receive that same award, particularly with this unbelievable class,” Iger said. 

	He later shared some words of encouragement for D’Amaro: “To Josh D’Amaro, you’re wearing that title really well. I am so proud to call you my successor.”

	Toward the end of his speech, Iger shared some love for all the talent he worked with during his time at Disney.

	“It’s not lost on me; I’m the executive in the room,” Iger said. “What executives typically do is they sign checks and they turn the lights on in the morning. I usually make coffee. But more than anything else, we’re around to support creators, the true talent that drives this company forward. Whether it’s producers like Jerry Bruckheimer, songwriters like Lin, or actors like Dwayne and Anne. I could go on and one. Singers, dancers, you name it. And so I accept this award for all of you.”

	Iger started his CEO trajectory in 1974 as a runner at ABC. He ascended to programming head and CEO at the network by 1996, when Disney acquired ABC and its parent company, Capital Cities. He was named CEO of the Walt Disney Company in 2005, succeeding Michael Eisner. That kicked off an historic run of transactions that power the company’s content today. Multi-billion acquisitions shepherded by Iger include Pixar in 2006, Marvel in 2009 and Lucasfilm in 2012.

	In 2021, Iger stepped down as CEO after an emergency extension related to COVID. His successor, Bob Chapek, was ousted in 2022, bringing Iger back into the fold. He officially resigned again as CEO at the top of 2026, succeeded by D’Amaro. Iger will remain a senior advisor and board member until the end of the year.

schema.headline: Bob Iger Gets All-Star Send-Off From Robert Downey Jr., Harrison Ford and New CEO Josh D’Amaro at D23 Disney Legends Ceremony

title: Ariana Grande Brings Out ‘Wicked’ Co-Star Cynthia Erivo for ‘Happy Days’ and ‘For Good’ at Eternal Sunshine London Show
description:
Ariana Grande brought out Cynthia Erivo to perform at her Aug. 16 Eternal Sunshine stop at London’s O2.

	The “Wicked” stars sang “For Good” and “Ha
body:
Ariana Grande brought out Cynthia Erivo to perform at her Aug. 16 Eternal Sunshine stop at London’s O2.

	The “Wicked” stars sang “For Good” and “Happy Days” on the second night in the U.K. for Grande’s tour.


	Grande is currently on her Eternal Sunshine Tour, which shares a title with her seventh studio album. The tour is scheduled to conclude with 10 dates at London’s O2 Arena, ending on Sept. 1.
	

	Following the conclusion of the tour, Grande will be taking a step back from public appearances. “She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny,” Grande’s rep told People in early August.


	Upon news of her break, it was also revealed that Grande dropped out of the West End revival of Stephen Sondheim’s “Sunday in the Park With George,” in which she was set to star alongside another “Wicked” alum, Jonathan Bailey.

	The “public scrutiny” has reached a fever pitch in recent years as Grande has been on a hectic run of promotion. Her physical appearance has been put under a microscope online. Her eighth studio album, “Petal,” was released on July 31. The music video for the title track, released concurrently, stirred up additional concerns about her physical appearance.

	Grande and Erivo starred in Jon M. Chu’s “Wicked” and its sequel “Wicked: For Good” as Glinda and Elphaba, respectively. After release of the first film, they both received Oscar nominations for their roles.

schema.headline: Ariana Grande Brings Out ‘Wicked’ Co-Star Cynthia Erivo for ‘Happy Days’ and ‘For Good’ at Eternal Sunshine London Show

title: Anne Hathaway Tears Up as She’s Named a Disney Legend (and Her 2026 Box Office Crosses $2 Billion): ‘I’m One of the Most Insanely Lucky People in the World’
description:
Shut up! Oscar winner Anne Hathaway is officially a Disney Legend. 

	Hathaway was officially inducted into Disney’s hall of fame on Sunday afternoo
body:
Shut up! Oscar winner Anne Hathaway is officially a Disney Legend. 

	Hathaway was officially inducted into Disney’s hall of fame on Sunday afternoon during D23, the company’s weekend-long ultimate fan event.

	“I am here today because I’m one of the most insanely lucky people in the world,” Hathaway said after her “Devil Wears Prada” director David Frankel and Vogue editor Anna Wintour introduced her to the stage, where she received a massive round of applause.
	

	“How lucky am I that I was born into a family where acting, storytelling and imagination were valued and celebrated,” she said, pointing out her parents in the audience. Hathaway was also joined by her husband Adam Shulman (who she confirms “makes her foot pop”) and their two sons, Jonathan and Jack.



	The honor comes 25 years after Hathaway made her big-screen debut as Mia Thermopolis in Disney’s “The Princess Diaries,” which hit theaters on Aug. 3, 2001. Her Disney legend continued with 2004’s “The Devil Wears Prada,” where she played Andy Sachs, assistant to the boss from hell at the glossy fashion magazine, Runway. Hathaway reprised that role earlier this year in “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” which grossed more than $690 million worldwide, bringing the franchise total above the $1 billion mark.

	Thus, Hathaway’s list of thank yous included the late Garry Marshall, who chose her to play the Genovian princess-to-be, as well as Debra Martin Chase and the late Whitney Houston, who produced the movie, which was once called “The Princess of Tribeca.”
	

	“How lucky am I that my first studio picture ever starred perhaps the greatest Disney Legend of all time, the incomparable Julie Andrews,” Hathaway said. “I learned so much from her when I was just 17. and from the time that I met her at the first readthrough, she showed me that kindness, patience, friendliness, graciousness, good humor and hard work were an unbeatable combination.”

	Luckily, that film, Hathaway said, became her first Disney classic – and Andrews’ 27th.

	“I’m so lucky that my first booking led to so many opportunities when I was still so young, [like] getting a job that a million girls were built for in ‘The Devil Wears Prada,'” Hathaway continued. “I got to be with Stanley Tucci. I got to be with Emily Blunt. I got to be with um…oh what’s her name,” she said, pretending to forget Meryl Streep’s name. “I’ve gotten to spend my life so far, doing what I love, having so many adventures along the way, knowing joy and valuing the extraordinary good fortune that allows me to share my life with my greatest blessing — a family I couldn’t love more.”

	“Prada” director Frankel presented Hathaway with the honor, telling the crowd how the studio originally wanted another actress for the role. “Thank God for Meryl Streep,” Frankel said. “She saw Annie’s performance in ‘Brokeback Mountain’ and said, ‘Yeah, this girl.’ Game recognizes game.” 

	Then, Wintour appeared via video to pay tribute to the star. “Over the years, I’ve gotten to know Anne as an ideal front row companion, as well as a perfect theater date,” Wintour said. “But I recently had the chance to do a small comedy routine with her at the Oscars. Which, I confess, was a little like stepping onto the dance floor with Fred Astaire. Fortunately, Anne made it incredibly easy for me, which is something she seems to do for everyone, at every time. There is so much to admire about Anne: her work ethic, her talent, her versatility, but most of all, it’s her kindness that is so impressive.”

Anna Wintour honors Anne Hathaway as a Disney Legend at #D23, saying that nobody deserves it more:“She is an amazing actress, but also a devoted mother, a loving wife, and the very best of friends. Nobody deserves the Disney Legends Award more than you.” pic.twitter.com/25jA3mIyG6— Variety (@Variety) August 16, 2026


	Joining Hathaway in the Disney Legends class of 2026 are former Disney CEO Bob Iger, Dwayne Johnson, the Jonas Brothers, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Alan Tudyk, producer Jerry Bruckheimer, sportscaster Chris Berman, animator Eric Goldberg, Imagineer Kim Irvine and stage and voice actress Susan Egan.
	

	Sunday afternoon’s ceremony was Hathaway’s second trip to Anaheim this weekend for D23. She made a surprise appearance at the Disney Entertainment Showcase on Friday night to share an update on the long-awaited threequel “Princess Diaries 3,” which is expected to continue the story following the 2004 sequel “Royal Engagement” rather than reboot the franchise.

	“I very often feel like I’m having the luckiest life because my first film was embraced so completely by an audience that took it so deep into their hearts, and they’ve never let it go,” Hathaway told Variety last Sunday at the premiere of “The End of Oak Street” for Warner Bros. “My mom is always sending me pictures, like, ‘Oh, my friend’s daughter had a “Princess Diaries” engagement party.’ And so it’s become this something far bigger than the film, something far bigger than me, certainly.”

	“I know it sounds like such a diplomatic, political thing to say, but it truly is the privilege of my life to have been a part of something that has become a part of other people’s lives. It feels like it’s more than just a film,” she continued. “Outside of my family, movies are the thing that I love most in this world. So I’m happy when I know that I’m in a community full of people that love movies and love them as deeply as I do.”

	2026 has been a massive year for Hathaway, who stars in five movies, including “The End of Oak Street,” which hit theaters on Friday. The dinosaur action movie grossed $47 million on opening weekend, bringing Hathaway’s box office haul for the year over $2 billion, factoring in “The Odyssey” (which has grossed $1.29 billion and counting), “Mother Mary” ($3 million), “The End of Oak Street” and “The Devil Wears Prada 2.” Hathaway’s fifth and final film of the year, “Verity,” an adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s chiller, debuts on October 2. (Hathaway’s “Odyssey” co-stars Zendaya, Tom Holland and Bennie Safdie also crossed the box office milestone this year.)

	“It’s overwhelming. It’s a joy, and it’s incredible,” Hathaway said about this uber-successful season. “Having done this for as long as I have, I know the rarity of being in such a wide variety of films this year, so I feel incredibly fortunate that that’s been my experience.”



	

					Anne Hathaway onstage at the Disney Entertainment Showcase at D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event in Anaheim, California.
									Getty Images for Disney

schema.headline: Anne Hathaway Tears Up as She’s Named a Disney Legend (and Her 2026 Box Office Crosses $2 Billion): ‘I’m One of the Most Insanely Lucky People in the World’

title: Noah Kahan Turns His ‘Miserable’ Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review
description: “My name is Noah Kahan and I am here to make you fucking miserable!” the biggest male rock star on the charts right now announced almost at the outs
body:
“My name is Noah Kahan and I am here to make you fucking miserable!” the biggest male rock star on the charts right now announced almost at the outset of his sold-out show Saturday night at Pasadena’s Rose Bowl Stadium. In this, he was unsuccessful, but to Kahan’s credit, he did not really try very hard to turn the 57,000-strong crowd into a miserablists’ convention. There was some truth ungirding Kahan’s introductory joke, given how much of the song catalog that has made him a superstar is devoted to what he would call “intrusive thoughts” about disconnection, loneliness and unworthiness. But the celebrative spirit of the two-and-a-half-hour show kept all of those undercurrents at bay, to maybe be better experienced when you’re back home, just the records and you and your neurodivergence. In concert, Kahan’s about nothing but putting on a pure jubilee — as good a time as you’re likely to have in any concert venue, large or small, in 2026.
	

	L.A. locals will remember that he was easily selling out two nights at the Hollywood Bowl in mid-2024, so his instantaneous sellout of the Rose Bowl isn’t that much further of a leap. (He probably could have sold out two here, too, if the tour planners had left room for multi-nighters in his schedule.) But this wave of Kahan-mania hasn’t been going on for so long that we can’t still be impressed and maybe even puzzled by the sheer unlikeliness of it. Humble singer-songwriter comes along singing about bare trees, cold morning drives, dead friends, divorced parents and all the uncertainties anyone in his twenties in the most forlorn parts of the Northeast could face, and suddenly he’s as big as BTS? Go figure. You get the sense from Kahan that he hasn’t completely figured out himself what went so right in singing so much feel-wrong music: “I remember playing at the Troubadour and being happy if that was the rest of my career,” he told the massive crowd. “I’m grateful as fuck to be here with y’all.” That’s a common sentiment from a touring superstar, but there’s a sense that Kahan really might be as happily bewildered as the rest of us about how songs this personal and cloudy came to captivate even sunny California.  
	

	Anyway, he’s good — really, really, really good – so that’s a gift horse we won’t look in the mouth. As far as pop stars who happen to also be thoughtful and excellent songwriters go, Kahan is in the upper ranks. If anything, he’s underrated, at least by some of the cognoscenti, who tend not to know how to think about it when something that falls loosely under the rubrick of Americana makes it big, other than to mark it down as some sort of curious throwback to Mumford & Sons’ stomp-and-holler folk-rock mini-revolution. It is partially that, but Kahan is also really a contemporary to Taylor Swift, in the way that he fills his songs with peculiarly personal details that leave fans hanging on every lyric, on the way to doing satisfying stadium romps where the faithful will shout back every long-memorized random aside. (Not right in your ear, if you’re lucky.) He’d probably get more credit for just how strong the writing is if he’d stayed in a proper niche, but some overnight sensations can’t be helped.



	

					Noah Kahan performs with Chappell Roan at Rose Bowl Stadium in Pasadena, California on August 15, 2026.
									Patrick McCormack
	



	His most recent album, “The Great Divide,” is one of the year’s most commercially sturdy records, not having been out of the top 10 since it debuted in April and not likely to leave any time soon. The 20-track (in its deluxe version) set might be even stronger in its storytelling than the star-making “Stick Season,” so it was not to the Rose Bowl set’s detriment at all that he performed 14 of its tracks. One of those songs, “Orbiter,” is about his experience at the 2024 Grammys, feeling like a loser when he lost the best new artist category to Victoria Monet. (Remarkably, that’s one of just two Grammy categories Kahan has even been up for, the other being as a featured artist on someone else’s country song. ) Being back in the greater L.A. area for this show, he used the Rose Bowl as his confessional.

	“This is not gonna endear me to the crowd,” Kahan said, gearing up to explain why this is not his favorite city. “L.A. has been home to some of the worst days of my life and my music career. I’m sorry, it’s not your guys’ fault, but I’ve always felt a little out of place here… I always felt like when I came here I was auditioning for something, even though I wasn’t. I never felt like I fit… I got my feelings so hurt by losing awards and losing things and feeling like I was entitled to shit that I wasn’t entitled to. None of us are entitled to anything in this business, or in our lives, really. Um, and I thought about why I wanted to keep going, and it was for my wife, my mom, and it was for you all. So this is a song about you three — my three best friends.”
	



	

					Noah Kahan performs at Rose Bowl Stadium in Pasadena, California on August 15, 2026.
									Patrick McCormack
	



	In the fairy-tale version of this story, his team would submit his song about losing a Grammy, and it would win a Grammy. That won’t happen, not least of all because there are more obvious focus tracks than “Orbiter” to put in for possible nominations. Even then, who knows if Recording Academy voters will be yet ready to give him his due? If “The Great Divide” doesn’t get much Grammy love, it might only help further drive his art. Kahan seems to thrive, on this latest album, on exploring some of the vagaries that come with getting a lot of attention, and how it affects relationships with family and old friends and even (maybe) especially his own self-image. And it’s pretty interesting stuff. There have been a number of albums this year that go into the side effects of fame — Ariana Grande’s in a big way, Phoebe Bridgers’ to a lesser extent — but no one is quite so humble or conflicted about it as Kahan. He projects himself onto old acquaintances or family members, laying into him in ways it’s unlikely very many of them have in real life. One song that was a big hit Saturday night, “Dashboard,” is a song in which, effectively, he inhabits the role of someone who is calling Noah Kahan an asshole for four minutes. It’s endearing and very catchy, even if perhaps the asshole in question doth protest too much.

	In reality, Kahan’s ascent strikes people as a case of good guys finishing first… as they always do, right? I was struck by how Chappell Roan characterized him when he brought her out to duet at the Rose Bowl. Her surprise appearance late in the set was so that they could trade verses and harmonize on the choruses of her song “California,” a ballad that shares some themes of dislocation and dissociation that are common to Kahan’s own geographically specific songs. As recognition of her red tresses turned into a roar, Kahan sang Roan’s praises, describing “California” as “the first song I ever heard of Kayleigh’s, and the reason I fell in love with her music. And I’m just really proud of her.”



	

					Noah Kahan and Chappell Roan at the Rose Bowl Stadium
									Patrick McCormack
	



	Roan returned the appreciation, saying, “Noah always stands up for me, seriously.” (Fans likely understood this to reference how, in March, Kahan publicly had her back when Roan was taking some flack for protesting the aggressiveness of professional autograph scalpers.) Roan doubled down on Kahan’s virtue: “He’s a good person — for real.” Now, “good person” may not be as reliable a way to trump up a rock star as something, like, say, “bad-ass,” but we have the feeling his career will survive the rumors of his virtue.
	

	A few things have changed since Kahan headlined the Bowl two years ago, besides the major infusion of “Great Divide” songs. For one thing, there were fewer extended comic monologues, which I missed, though I wouldn’t argue that any of the 27 songs in the set should be tossed out for the sake of a funny story. Kahan may be figuring that he gets to exercise that muscle enough on social media, or that his fans have already heard plenty abut his family dynamics, whether in past tour patter or in his excellent recent Netflix documentary, “Noah Kahan: Out of Body,” which went in a lot deeper than a moment’s anecdote could. Anyway, he was witty enough, and telling enough, in passing. In “All My Love,” a new song where he catches an old friend or lover up on recent developments in his life, he sings of his amicably divorced parents, “My folks still talk, but they speak in these two-word sentences.” In concert, he found time before the next line to quickly add: “And now they’re up to seven-word sentences!”

	Kahan’s voice is one of the things about him that may be underrated. He sounds like he’s constantly on the verge of breaking into a falsetto, but not quite needing to go there, although if he does, it’s as sweet and expressive as you’d hope. As with a lot of singers we take for granted, you don’t really think about how strong he is until something goes amiss. There was just such a moment in Saturday’s show, when he went to sing “Pain Is Cold Water” — a touching acoustic song that he only does occasionally, acoustically, on the C-stage — and his voice cracked in the very first line. “Oh my God!” he blurted, stopping it and starting again to give it a fighting chance. It proceeded flawlessly from there, with Kahan almost apologizing for how slick it turned out. “Sorry to go all Christina Aguilera on you after sounding like a 13-year-old boy,” he joked.

	The biggest difference from his “Stick Season” touring, anyhow, is — surprise — production values. This tour has a nifty conceit: a physical rooftop that cyclically fell and rose to provide the roofline for different structures that changed as a result of digital projections combined with pillars and/or porches that stagehands would bring out. At first it was a cabin he and his six-piece band would perform in front of, with an old beater of a Volvo parked outside. Later on, the cabin became a general store, and the car turned into a Vermont police cruiser — just in time, inevitably, for one of his signature songs, “Dial Drunk.” This presumably fictional tale of a DUI arrest was dramatized (or comedicized) with a trooper actually slamming Kahan against the hood, followed by cameras catching just the right angle on him inside the vehicle as he lamented the girlfriend who would not pick up. Aside from a few agreeable band poses, “Dial Drunk” was the only time of the night there was anything that might be considered schtick… and in a stadium setting, it’s hard to begrudge that crowd-pleasing of a moment.
	

	By contrast, when the braided star went up onto the hovering rooftop to sing a single number atop the prop with his acoustic guitar, “Willing and Able,” he seemed to be having a genuinely emotional moment, which much of the quieted crowd definitely observed. If he was just acting his way through that number, no harm done. Either way, it says a lot that Kahan would take one of the quietest numbers from the sprawling “Great Divide” and make a somber, solitary place for it in his big rock show, trusting that the subtle storytelling about two old friends uneasily dancing around their resentments and suspicions will be intutively understood or embraced by a crowd of tens of thousands. Violin player Nina de Vitry provided an especially tasteful complement on this ballad, making one fiddle sound like a whole string section.

	Kahan also made sure to give solo spots to the rest of his accomplished ensemble — Zubin Thakkar, Dylan Jones, Alex Bachari, Marcos Valles and Mike Harris. The six-piece backing crew turned into a nine-piece when they were joined for the three encore numbers by a three-person horn section, allowing the music to take on a Springsteenian/”Wrecking Ball” quality for the extended finale.



	

					Noah Kahan performs at Rose Bowl Stadium in Pasadena, California on August 15, 2026.
									Patrick McCormack
	



	The way Kahan was able to choreograph this fiddle- and banjo-laden group across different parts of the stage to visually elongate the party was reminiscent of what another player in the superstar-Americana space, Zach Bryan, has done with the players at his stadium shows. But any thinking about similarities along those lines inevitably leads to thinking about how fundamentally different Bryan’s and Kahan’s personalities are. Bryan is sympathetic but still surly… or at least his offstage shenanigans lead you to feel he could pop off without a lot of provocation. Kahan, on the other hand, is absolutely your BFF… and the worst thing he is going to do is ghost you, and then come back to town and apologize for ghosting you, and then write a song about how he knows you resent him for patronizing you, because he’s empathetic that way. Very important distinction there.

	Kahan is one of the good guys not least of all because of the honest ways in which he talks about substance abuse recovery and mental health, with songs that do such a bravura job of exploring what it is like to, as he says, have a busy head. We probably shouldn’t judge artists by the signs that fans bring to their performances, but I had to take some amusement when the cameras at the Rose Bowl began showing glimpses of the fans down front during some of the final songs of Saturday’s show. Instead of asking for a request or a hug or a birthday shout-out, the camera caught a young woman holding up a big, wordy sign that read, in part: “Thank you for breaking the chain of generational trauma!” 
	

	A different kind of artist calls for a different kind of fandom… a therapeutized one that knows manic elation when they see it.

schema.headline: Noah Kahan Turns His ‘Miserable’ Material Into Manic Elation at Triumphant Rose Bowl Stadium Show: Concert Review

title: ‘Lanterns’ Premiere Shocker: Stars Kyle Chandler, Aaron Pierre and Show Creators Break Down That Time Jump and Cliffhanger
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 1 premiere of “Lanterns,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	What kind of superhero show has t
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 1 premiere of “Lanterns,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	What kind of superhero show has the guts to kill off its lead character in the first episode?

	Of course, just because Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) is found dead in the bleachers by John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) and town sheriff Kerry (Kelly MacDonald) in the middle of a brutal 2026 winter doesn’t mean audiences won’t get to see Green Lantern in action in future episodes — the show sets up a non-linear structure that jumps among different storylines from the very opening scene, which begins in 1996 and sets up a young John’s connection to taking the Green Lantern mantle.
	

	But clueing audiences in on the fact that the  show’s protagonist’s days are numbered is bold for the comic book genre. And it makes for one hell of a cliffhanger for the series premiere.


	“Whether it’s the right cliffhanger or not is basically in the hands of the audience now,” “Lanterns” co-creator Damon Lindelof tells Variety. “But one of the very first things that was part of the premise was that this is a murder mystery with Green Lantern solving it, and then you sort of start at, ‘Well, who gets murdered and why are we supposed to care about them?’ The more that we talked about it, the more that it kept coming back to the idea of, ‘What if it was one of them?'”

	“Lanterns,” the latest show under James Gunn and Peter Safran’s newly expanded DCU, follows Hal as he is forced to take John under his wing. As the Green Lantern, Hal has the power to create material items through his ring, and acts as an intergalactic space officer protecting humanity from extraterrestrial threats. Things take a dark turn, however, after a series of unexplainable deaths draw Hal and John to a small town in Nebraska.
	

	When Chandler first read the ending of the episode, he “cheered” at Hal’s demise.

	“Not just for the storyline and all that, but what a way great way to end the first episode of this show,” Chandler says.

	MacDonald, who says Frances McDormand’s Oscar-winning performance in “Fargo” informed the way she played the sheriff just trying to keep her small town from falling apart, dreaded filming the scene when she discovers Hal’s dead body. “Just the thought of what was going to happen, I did not look forward to it. It was quite emotional, seeing him like that,” she says.



	

	



	Lindelof, who created HBO’s Emmy-winning “Watchmen” TV series that released in 2019 — bringing a grounded approach to it — recognizes the opportunity to subvert audience expectations from what they’ve come to expect in the genre.

	“That you basically watched eight episodes and everybody had an adventure, and then at the end of the adventure, it’s just time for the next adventure,” Lindelof says. “So the idea that it would have real emotional stakes [was important]. But most importantly, this is a story about a guy who doesn’t want to give up the ring — and a guy who wants the ring. And it was important for us to message to the audience that we weren’t gonna try to have our cake and eat it too.”

	The episode sets up Hal and John’s budding mentor-mentee dynamic in a 2016 timeline, with Hal being a reluctant teacher. The tension between them comes to a head after the two arrive in Nebraska and begin investigating a school shooting that Hal believes is a front for aliens.

	“There’s a moment where we’re in the stands and we were literally this close. And it was a moment very early in their dynamic. Everything in John wants to just rumble in that moment, but he can’t and Hal knows he can’t,” Pierre says. “It was just so fun.”

	“It’s like making fun of the animals at the zoo behind the plate of glass,” Chandler adds with a laugh. “He’s can’t touch me, but I can do what I want!”

	Chandler says Hal has a deep respect for John from the beginning, even if it’s unspoken. “I knew that he could literally grab my neck and snap it,” he says.

	Seeing Chandler sit up on a pair of bleachers overlooking a football field may give viewers who were introduced to the Emmy-winning actor with “Friday Night Lights” a feeling of déjà vu. Chandler felt those memories for the series that turns 20 this fall.
	

	“There’s no doubt when I walked out there, it was a lot of different thoughts and emotions going through me,” Chandler says — although he never asked the writers if the callback was intentional.

	Overall, Pierre commends the “Lanterns” writers’ room, and is excited to see how the show’s weekly release model will play into the conversations fans have online.

	“They leave you — ‘want’ doesn’t even feel like a strong enough word. It’s needing to know what happens next,” Pierre says, teasingly. “I imagine there are going to be a few weeks where audiences are, in the healthiest, most excitable way, furious that they don’t know what is coming next.”

            Perez Hilton is still in the hospital nearly two weeks after his frightening live stream ... his family announced -- and his site is set to return to regularly scheduled programming.
      
    
            In an update on Perez's celebrity gossip website, his family tells fans that he is still in the hospital after the August 4 TikTok Live -- but they specify that he is in an inpatient setting getting the care he needs from both physicians and mental health professionals.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Inpatient mental health care can sometimes indicate a longer stay where patients remain hospitalized for extended periods of time while they recuperate -- while we don't know if this is the case for Perez, we do know his team will resume uploading celeb stories to his site.
      

            TMZ confirmed that Perez was treated for an overdose and multiple injuries on August 4, after authorities responded to reports of a possible suicide attempt at his home before he was transported to the hospital ... according to the police report.

[Perez] was standing in front of the shower, naked, cut up, covered in blood, with a box cutter in his hand."
      
    
            Another shocking detail about Perez's live stream has come to light this week ... his family confirmed his children, niece, and sister were all home as he was "experiencing a severe mental health crisis and harming himself" -- but his sister confirmed "they immediately fled to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma."

            Two of the ladies caught up in the viral fight at ritzy Beverly Hills steakhouse Steak 48 are serving up their side of the beef ... explaining exactly how a birthday celebration turned into a throwdown.
      
    
            The night started innocently enough, the women tell TMZ ... one of them heard men at a nearby table speaking Arabic and struck up a conversation -- and one of the men later came over and offered to cover their bill.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            They say another woman was already approaching the table when he made the offer ... and then sat on his lap.
      

            When the men were ready to leave, one asked them to tell the woman to get off his friend's lap. They tell us they passed along the request -- and got a physical response ... claiming the woman came up from behind swinging and pulling hair.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            They say that led to a few punches in return ... with her getting "socked" several times.
      
    
            The women deny anyone jumped her ... noting she was briefly placed in handcuffs that night but ultimately released.
      
    
            Despite all that, they say they wish the other fighter the best ... just don't expect them to break bread again anytime soon.

            Johnny and Tyler entered the MTV world together as roommates on the 2006 season of "The Real World" before repeatedly crossing paths on "The Challenge." After years as competitors, they teamed up and won "The Challenge: Rivals" in 2011.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Tyler was found dead Tuesday inside the bathtub of his Grand Forks, North Dakota apartment after a downstairs neighbor reported water leaking through the ceiling. He was 44.
      
    
            Police said there were no outward signs of trauma and preliminary findings showed no indication of homicide ... his cause of death remains under investigation.
